label: <DEL> step in long sequences (L>=7), plus last original token when L=9
explanation: A position/length unit that fires at the delimiter step when the sequence is long (L >= 7, so t >= 7). It never fires before step 7, whatever the tokens. About 76% of activation mass sits on <DEL>. Activation is strongest (near max) at <DEL> for L=8 and L=9, which fire on almost every sequence. It is weaker and less reliable at <DEL> for L=7 (about 65% of those sequences; low-quartile examples are mostly L=7). For L=9 it also fires on the last original token (t=8, about 99% of sequences, typically 0.6-0.8 of max), and occasionally (about 17%) on the last original token for L=8. Small spillover goes to the first copy step (t = L+1, about 0.1-0.3 of max) and a few earlier tokens at t=7. It does not fire on short sequences (L <= 6), on early original tokens, or past the first copy output. Token identity barely matters.

issues: The claim that the unit fires on the last original token in about 17% of L=8 sequences is wrong. (L==8)&(t==7) has test precision 0.082, so it is about 8%. (L==9)&(t==7), the second-to-last token, fires at the same rate (0.083), which the explanation leaves out.

The claim that 'token identity barely matters' is false for <DEL> at L=7, where firing depends strongly on tokens. Firing rate by prev_tok: z 0.88 vs u 0.16 vs w 0.33. By orig(0): w 0.86 vs x 0.21 vs i 0.48. For L>=8 the claim holds, because <DEL> fires there with precision 1.0.
The spillover onto the first copy step comes almost entirely from L=9 (about 7% of sequences). For L=8 it is about 0.2%. This is minor.

Misses on the test split are not systematic and hold only 1% of activation mass. They are mostly t=7 for L=8/9 plus first-copy spillover. The false positives are a single class: <DEL> at L=7 that falls below threshold (about 34%), which the explanation already admits.
Adding a token filter on L=7 <DEL> only raises test F1 from 0.926 to 0.932, so the existing predicate is essentially enough.
